bless.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: the priest, the parent, or the speaker does something (*blesses the fleet*, *blessed the ground*). No stative or linking use.
bless.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory, whether a person, an object, or a place: *she blesses the children*, ✗ *her mother blesses* is incomplete. The interjection *bless you* is a fixed fragment, not an ordinary intransitive.
bless.passive: **yes** — *the ground was blessed before a single shovel went in*, *that chapel has been blessed by three bishops*. Sense 3 exists only in the passive: *we have been blessed with patient neighbors*, with no active ✗ *something blessed us with neighbors*.

burn.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event runs both ways (*the shed burned* / *vandals burned the shed*). Not stative and not linking, though *burn with shame* takes a prepositional complement rather than an object.
burn.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when the thing itself is alight or reddening (*dry pine burns fast*, *I burn in fifteen minutes*, *the bulb burned out*), transitive when someone or something consumes it (*they burned the shed*, *he burned his hand*, *the furnace burns a gallon an hour*).
burn.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the shed was burned to the ground*, *a backup disc has been burned for every project*. Sense 9 is essentially passive-only: *investors got burned*, *I have been burned by contractors twice*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *fifteen minutes is burned in by me*.

chap.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative like *burn*: skin chaps, or wind chaps it. No stative or linking use; the very common *chapped* in *chapped lips* is the participle doing adjective duty.
chap.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with the skin or surface as subject (*my hands chapped badly*, *the clay chapped into plates*), transitive with the cold or the weather as subject (*wind like this chaps your face*).
chap.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but rare, because the participle is normally an adjective instead: *her knuckles were chapped* is read as a state, not as an event, and the agentive *her face was chapped by the wind* is possible but stiff. No passive of the intransitive ✗ *it was chapped by my hands*.

clap.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, and abrupt by definition (*clapped a hand over her mouth*). No stative or linking use.
clap.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the applause sense, alone or with *for* (*the whole room claps*, *they clapped for her*), transitive elsewhere: *clapped me on the shoulder*, *clapped a hand over her mouth*, *clapped him in jail*, *clapped eyes on the house*.
clap.passive: **restricted** — fine where a person is affected: *he was clapped in jail before his lawyer heard about it*, *players get clapped on the back after a bad inning*. The applause sense has no passive (intransitive), and the idiom resists one: ✗ *eyes were clapped on the house*.

dip.verb type: action — dynamic. Transitive senses are agentive (*dip bread in the oil*); the intransitive ones describe a brief downward movement of numbers or terrain (*sales dipped*, *the road dips*). No stative or linking use.
dip.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the immersion and lowering senses (*he dips his bread*, *ships dip their flags*, *she dipped water from the barrel*), intransitive in the decline and slope senses (*the temperature dipped below freezing*) and in *dip into* (*we dipped into savings*).
dip.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the whole tray of strawberries has been dipped in chocolate*, *the flag was dipped as they passed*. No passive of the fall or slope senses: ✗ *below freezing was dipped by the temperature*.

dwell.verb type: action in *dwell on*, a sustained mental activity that takes the progressive freely (*he's dwelling on it again*); closer to **stative** in the literary *live, reside* and *be lodged in* senses, which describe a standing situation (*they dwell in a cabin*, *a resentment dwelt in him*) and sit awkwardly in the progressive.
dwell.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense — the verb never takes a bare object and always leans on a preposition: *dwell on one bad review*, *dwell in that valley*, *dwell in him*. ✗ *She dwelt the subject* is impossible.
dwell.passive: **restricted** — no ordinary passive, since there is no object; only the formal prepositional passive of sense 1 is available: *the budget was dwelt on far too long*. The residence senses have none at all: ✗ *the cabin is dwelt in by them*.

enwrap.verb type: action — dynamic, the literary twin of *wrap*: fog, cloth, or darkness closes over something (*silence has enwrapped the valley*). No stative or linking use.
enwrap.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory, usually with *in*: *she enwrapped the child in a quilt*, ✗ *museums enwrap before they ship* is incomplete.
enwrap.passive: **yes**, and sense 2 lives in the passive: *he was enwrapped in the argument and never heard the bell*. Sense 1 passivizes normally too — *fragile pieces are enwrapped in acid-free tissue before shipping*.

indwell.verb type: **stative** — it reports presence within, not an act, so the progressive is out as a verb (✗ *grace is indwelling the believer*); the *-ing* form survives only as an adjective (*the indwelling Spirit*, *an indwelling catheter*).
indwell.transitivity: **transitive** — the thing inhabited is a direct object with no preposition: *grace indwells the believer*, *a stubbornness indwelt every sentence she wrote*.
indwell.passive: **restricted** — the participial passive is standard inside theology (*believers indwelt by the Spirit*), but a full clausal passive is rare and the extended sense resists it: ✗ *every sentence was indwelt by a quiet stubbornness*.

learn.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, including the mental ones, and it takes the progressive freely (*she's learning Spanish*, *we're still learning*). Not stative, despite naming a change in what you know.
learn.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a subject, skill, text, or *that*-clause (*he learned Spanish*, *she learned the whole part*, *they learned that the grant would not be renewed*), intransitive when the object is understood (*kids learn fast*, *he never learned*). Nonstandard sense 6 is even ditransitive: *his uncle learned him to shoot* — dialect only, ✗ in standard prose.
learn.passive: **restricted** — natural with a text or skill and no agent (*the lines were learned in four days*, *three new pieces have been learned this season*), and the *find out* sense passivizes impersonally in news style (*it was learned Friday that the grant would not be renewed*). A *by*-phrase is stilted: ✗ *Spanish was learned by him in eight months*.

misspell.verb type: action — dynamic, a single-sense verb naming what the writer or the machine does (*autocorrect misspells her name*). No stative or linking use.
misspell.transitivity: **transitive** — the word or name is obligatory: *he misspelled "necessary" twice*, ✗ *the engraver has misspelled* leaves the sentence hanging.
misspell.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual way to say it, since the culprit rarely matters: *the donor's name was misspelled on the plaque*, *her last name has been misspelled on every form*.

nip.verb type: action — dynamic and momentary: a quick bite, a pinch, a sting of frost. No stative or linking use.
nip.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing bitten or removed (*a crab nipped his finger*, *frost nipped the tomatoes*, *nip the side shoots off*, *we nipped that rumor in the bud*), intransitive with *at* for a habit (*the puppy nips at your ankles*, *he nipped at a flask*) and in the British *nip out for milk*.
nip.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the tomatoes were nipped by frost*, *the rumor was nipped in the bud before it reached the board*. No passive of *nip at* or of the British *nip out*: ✗ *your ankles are nipped at by the puppy* is barely English.

relearn.verb type: action — dynamic, and effortful by definition; it takes the progressive readily (*she's relearning the fingering*). No stative or linking use.
relearn.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the skill, route, or lesson as object (*he relearned the fingering*, *the team had relearned the whole playbook*), and it also takes an infinitive (*stroke patients relearn to walk*). Object-free use is rare but possible: *at that age you relearn fast*.
relearn.passive: **yes**, though uncommon and usually agentless: *the whole playbook had to be relearned*, *that lesson gets relearned every generation*. A *by*-phrase is awkward: ✗ *the fingering was relearned by him*.

smell.verb type: Three classes in one entry. **Stative** in the perception sense — a state of the perceiver, so the progressive is out and *can* fills in: *I can smell rain*, ✗ *I am smelling smoke*. **Action** in the deliberate sense 2, which does take the progressive: *she's smelling the milk*. **Linking (copular)** in senses 3–4, joining subject to a complement rather than an object: *the apartment smelled like burnt popcorn*, *fresh basil smells wonderful*, *that cooler smells*.
smell.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the perception, sniffing, and figurative senses (*he smelled gas*, *she smells the milk*, *I smell a rat*), intransitive or copular in the give-off senses (*the room smells*, *it smells of paint*, *the plan smells of desperation*).
smell.passive: **restricted** — agentless report passives are fine (*smoke was smelled in the stairwell*), but the stative perception resists a *by*-phrase the way other perception verbs do: ✗ *rain is smelled by me before the clouds show*. The linking senses have no passive at all: ✗ *burnt popcorn was smelled like by the apartment*.

spell.verb type: action — dynamic in the letter, editorial, and relief senses (*spell it slowly*, *I'll spell you at the wheel*). Sense 3 is closer to **stative**: *another dry summer spells trouble* states a consequence rather than an act, and the progressive is odd there.
spell.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a word, outcome, or person as object (*she spelled the street name wrong*, *that memo spells doom*, *two neighbors spelled her at the hospital*), intransitive when the ability itself is the point (*he can't spell*, *spell slowly for me*).
spell.passive: **restricted** — routine in the letter and editorial senses (*the name was spelled wrong on the envelope*, *the penalty had been spelled out in the first paragraph*), but the *mean, signal* sense refuses it: ✗ *trouble is spelled by another dry summer*.

spill.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative: someone spills it, or it spills (*I spilled coffee* / *the contents spill*). No stative or linking use.
spill.transitivity: **both** — transitive and usually accidental with the liquid as object (*I spilled coffee on the keyboard*, *she spilled the whole story*, *the horse spilled him at the fence*), intransitive with the contents, crowd, or light as subject (*it spills every time you move it*, *fans spilled into the street*, *costs have spilled over*).
spill.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *juice has been spilled on the back seat*, *the details were spilled to a reporter*; the participle is fixed in *no use crying over spilled milk*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *the street was spilled into by fans*.

spoil.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative in the food sense (*the heat spoiled the cream* / *cream spoils fast*). No stative or linking use; *be spoiling for a fight* is an idiom locked in the *-ing* form, not a progressive you can unwind (✗ *he spoiled for a fight*).
spoil.transitivity: **both** — transitive when something or someone is ruined, indulged, or given away (*rain spoiled the game*, *her grandparents have spoiled those kids*, *don't spoil the twist*), intransitive of food going bad (*cream spoils fast in a warm car*).
spoil.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the finale has been spoiled for everybody*, *those kids have been spoiled since the day they were born*, *a spoiled ballot*. No passive of the food sense: ✗ *the cooler's contents were spoiled by themselves* — you say *the heat spoiled everything* or *everything spoiled*.

sunburn.verb type: action — dynamic, ergative like its base *burn*: skin sunburns, or the sun sunburns it. No stative or linking use, and in practice Americans reach for *get sunburned* rather than the finite verb.
sunburn.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with the person or the skin as subject (*pale skin sunburns in twenty minutes*, *we sunburn easily*), transitive with the body part as object (*he sunburned the back of his neck*, *years of roofing had sunburned his forearms*).
sunburn.passive: **restricted** — the participle is where the verb actually lives, and it reads as a state: *I got sunburned*, *the farmer's face was sunburned and lined*. An agentive passive is unnatural: ✗ *his neck was sunburned by the sun*.

toss.verb type: action — dynamic and quick in every sense, from the casual throw to the judge's dismissal (*the judge tossed the case*). No stative or linking use.
toss.transitivity: **both**, and **ditransitive** in the throwing sense — *toss me the keys*, *he tossed her the ball*. Otherwise transitive (*toss the receipt*, *toss the salad*, *she tossed her hair*, *an appeals court has tossed two charges*), intransitive in *toss and turn*, *the boat tossed all night*, and *we tossed for the top bunk*.
toss.passive: **yes** — *the case was tossed for lack of evidence*, *the salad should be tossed right before you serve it*, *a jacket has been tossed over the railing*. No passive of the restless-movement sense: ✗ *it was tossed and turned by him all night*.

unlearn.verb type: action — dynamic and deliberate; the entry insists the effort is the point, and the progressive is normal (*they're still unlearning the old form*).
unlearn.transitivity: **transitive** — a habit, skill, or belief is obligatory as object: *unlearn bad form*, *she unlearned the accent she grew up with*, ✗ *the players spent a month unlearning* is incomplete without one.
unlearn.passive: **yes**, though usually agentless — *bad form has to be unlearned before anything better goes in*, *that idea has been unlearned by a whole generation*. The active infinitive stays commoner: *some things are harder to unlearn than to learn*.

vex.verb type: action — a psychological verb with the experiencer as object (*slow permits vexed the developer*). Sense 2 shades **stative**, describing a standing condition of a problem (*the same question vexes every committee*), and the participle *vexed* has drifted into adjective territory in *a vexed question*.
vex.transitivity: **transitive** — the person or group troubled is obligatory: *it does not take much to vex him*, ✗ *small delays vex* is incomplete.
vex.passive: **yes** — *editors have been vexed by that inconsistency for years*, *mathematicians were vexed by the problem for a century*. The passive participle is in fact the commonest live form of the verb in American writing.

wrap.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, literal or figurative (*wrapped the leftovers*, *we wrapped up the audit*). No stative or linking use.
wrap.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the covering, winding, and finishing senses (*she wraps every gift*, *wrap the pipes*, *we wrapped up the audit*), intransitive in the film sense and in dressing warmly (*they wrap on Friday*, *wrap up — it's ten degrees out*).
wrap.passive: **yes** — *every gift is wrapped in plain brown paper*, *the shoot had been wrapped two days early*. Sense 6 is passive-only in form: *he was wrapped up in the game*, *she has been wrapped up in that manuscript for months*. The idiom in sense 7 refuses it: ✗ *the numbers can't be wrapped my head around*.
